narrative:
The model has analyzed your academic situation and determined that there’s a **22% chance** you might not pass your final year. While this isn’t a certainty, it’s high enough that the school has decided you should take extra remedial courses to help you succeed. Think of it like a warning sign—your current path has some risks, and these courses are a way to strengthen your foundation before the final push.

The decision isn’t random; it’s based on three key factors that stood out in your profile. First, the model noticed that **you haven’t had any past class failures**, which actually works in your favor—most students who struggle tend to have a history of failing subjects. This suggests your challenges might be more about consistency or external pressures than fundamental gaps in understanding.

However, two other aspects pushed the prediction toward risk. One is that **you’re not taking extra paid classes** in your main subjects. While most students manage without them, research shows that those who invest in additional help—even just a few hours a week—tend to perform better, especially in demanding courses. Since only a small fraction of students (just 3%) take these classes, your choice not to might mean you’re relying more on self-study or school support alone, which can be harder to balance.

The second factor is your **aspiration to pursue higher education**. This might sound counterintuitive—why would wanting to go further hurt your chances? Here’s the thing: students who *only* care about passing their current year sometimes take shortcuts or don’t push as hard. But students like you, who are already thinking ahead, often hold themselves to higher standards. That can create extra stress, especially if you’re juggling other responsibilities like family support or part-time work (which the model also picked up on). The pressure to excel might be making it harder to stay on top of everything.

The good news? These courses aren’t a punishment—they’re a chance to fill in any small gaps before they become bigger problems. Focus on using them to build confidence in areas where you might be stretching yourself too thin. And if you’re already balancing a lot, consider whether you’d benefit from even a little extra structured help outside of school. Small adjustments now could make the difference between just passing and truly thriving.
